newsitem.title: ITALY: Banco Napoli sale attracts third Italy name.
newsitem.headline: Banco Napoli sale attracts third Italy name.

text.p: Banco di Napoli's privatisation has attracted a third Italian name interested in the Treasury's sell-off but analysts on Monday said a combined three-way bid for the loss-making south Italian bank appears favourite to win.

Italian state-owned credit institute Mediocredito Centrale said it aims to submit a formal offer for the Naples-based bank, while Banco di Napoli's top management argue that Mediocredito Centrale would make a good partner with two other Italian parties in a joint bid.

In mid-November, the Banco di Napoli said three Italian and three foreign institutions had expressed an interest in Banco di Napoli in a process open to offers until December 20, although the Treasury has encouraged parties to bid by December 2.

Treasury-controlled Banca Nazionale de Lavoro and former state owned insurer INA have expressed joint interest in making a bid, while analysts can only speculate on the identity of the three non-Italian interested parties.

Banco di Napoli's top management, chairman Giuseppe Falcone and director general Federico Pepe, said in an interview in La Repubblica that a joint three-way bid for the 60 percent stake on offer would make a very competitive combination.

They argue that Mediocredito is involved in the south but does not have a network of branches, BNL -- 85 percent Treasury owned -- does not have a large presence in the south and INA, where the Treasury still has a 34 percent stake, offers the possibility of an accord between an insurance and banking group.
INA says its will decide on December 17 on a final bid according to one of its major shareholders San Paolo di Torino, itself Italy's largest banking group.
"A three-way bid makes sense and if it results in a leaner and smaller Banco di Napoli it could ultimately make a good bank," said one leading banking analyst at a Milan broker.

He said its success would depend on achieving lower labour costs, reaching an efficient day-to-day management structure and agreeing what interest payments would be due on the group's bad debts payable to Reviban, which was set up to take over most of the Neapolitan group's poor or doubtful loans.

But some analysts are not so convinced that this is a winning formula and say that although the bank is being cleansed of its bad debts the group still needs restructuring and the strong, rigour our leadership of a successful independent bank.

Hopes had been high that a well-managed rich northern Italian bank would come to the rescue of Banco di Napoli, but early fovourites Banco Ambrosiano Veneto and Banca Commerciale Italiana have said they are not interested in making a bid.

Analysts are doubtful that a foreign bid will emerge in a fragmented Italian market with limited non-Italian involvement, many banks still held by charity foundations or by the state. There are nearly 1,000 different banking groups throughout Italy.
"For a northern European banking group there must be far better investments than in a loss-making bank in southern Italy, which northern banks won't touch," said one London analyst.
Banco di Napoli unveiled a record loss of 3.12 trillion lire ($2.1 billion) in 1995, and plunged a further 674 billion lire into the red in the first half of this year.

Since the announcement of interest from foreign banks, a string of banks have denied any interest in Banco di Napoli including Britain's National Westminster Bank, Germany's Bayerische Landesbank, and Dutch Rabobank Nederland BV. ($1=1,516 lire)
